reference_title: Design and Construction of Driven Pile Foundations

sections.title: Cranes
sections.summary: The driving system both installs the pile and measures its resistance; crane, leads, hammer and helmet are the primary components. Crawler cranes: mobile, stable, 360 degree swing, counterweight power pack, trucked in pieces, need firm ground or mats. Truck cranes travel on their own but cannot walk with loads. Rough terrain cranes set up fast but have restricted side lifting.
sections.body: 15.1 Cranes (pp. 333 to 336). Chapter intro: installing piles means choosing the most cost effective equipment to reach the specified depth without damage in the least time; the driving system is also a measuring instrument for nominal resistance, so the engineer and contractor must know suitable equipment and confirm it operates properly. Crane, leads, hammer and helmet are the primary components; followers, jetting, predrilling and spudding may be permitted. Photographs courtesy GRL Engineers unless noted. Cranes: crawler cranes, historically most common, have good mobility and stability from a wide base, are easily walked, can carry a hydraulic power pack or compressor as counterweight, swing 360 degrees, but are trucked in pieces, assembled by another crane, and need firm ground or crane mats (Figure 15-1). Truck or mobile cranes travel under their own power and set up simply but cannot walk with heavy loads, so moving between substructures usually means laying down and detaching hammer and leads; outriggers level them; the power source cannot be crane mounted; side lifting is restricted (Figure 15-2). Rough terrain cranes set up and relevel quickly, can sometimes walk with loads over the front, are more mobile than truck cranes in difficult terrain, but have very restricted side lifting and no crane-mounted power source (Figure 15-3).
key_points: Driving system is both installation tool and measuring instrument for nominal resistance
Primary components: crane, leads, hammer and helmet
Crawler cranes: stable, walkable, 360 degree swing; trucked in pieces; need firm ground or mats
Truck cranes cannot walk with loads; rough terrain cranes have very restricted side lifting

sections.title: Dedicated and Universal Rigs
sections.summary: Dedicated and universal rigs carry a telescoping leader raised hydraulically from transport to driving position, so setup needs no additional heavy equipment; their winch lines offload and loft piles.
sections.body: 15.2 Dedicated and Universal Rigs (pp. 336 to 338). Use of dedicated and universal rigs has increased: a telescoping leader is moved from horizontal transport to vertical driving position by hydraulic support arms, so setup is fast without other heavy equipment, and winch lines offload piles and loft them beneath the hammer. Figure 15-4 shows a dedicated system with a hydraulic hammer, Figure 15-5 a universal rig with a diesel hammer.
key_points: Telescoping leader raised hydraulically: fast setup without extra heavy equipment
Winch lines offload and loft piles into position

sections.title: Leads
sections.summary: Leads keep hammer and pile aligned for concentric blows. Box leads most common; swinging leads (most widely used: simple, light, cheap, largest radius; preferable in excavations or over water when embedded and gated); fixed leads with spotter (moonbeam for side batter); semi-fixed or vertical travel leads; offshore leads with a template. Keep a pile gate at the bottom.
sections.body: 15.3 Leads (pp. 338 to 347). Leads maintain hammer-pile alignment so each blow is concentric; box leads are most common (Figure 15-6). Configurations: swinging, fixed, semi-fixed or vertical travel, offshore. Swinging leads (Figure 15-7), most widely used for simplicity, lightness and low cost, hang from the boom on straps with the hammer on a crane line (a) or, most commonly, leads and hammer on separate lines (b); they rotate to align without precise crane alignment and allow the largest operating radius (Figures 15-1, 15-2). A stabbing guide at the bottom (Figure 15-8) is dropped into the ground and the boom set for verticality or batter. Historic penalties or prohibitions on swinging leads are not justified: they are preferable in excavations or over water, and if long enough to embed firmly with a bottom gate (Figure 15-9) bottom alignment is held; keep the free line between boom tip and lead top short. Batter piles are harder to align, worse with diesel hammers whose starting pulls the pile out of line. Fixed leads connect to the boom point and to the crane by a spotter or brace (Figures 15-10, 15-11), holding true alignment but slower to reposition. Semi-fixed or vertical travel leads allow vertical movement at the boom and brace connections (Figure 15-12). Fixed leads handle plumb or in-line batter piles; side batter needs a moonbeam (Figure 15-13). Offshore leads are short sections with a pile guide that align the hammer only, with a template holding the pile (templates are in 15.4, though the text says 'Section 15.3'; Figures 15-14, 15-15, 15-3). In all cases avoid eccentric impacts; use a pile gate at the bottom.
key_points: Leads keep hammer and pile aligned for concentric impact
Swinging leads: most widely used; preferable in excavations or over water when embedded and gated
Fixed leads with spotter hold alignment; moonbeam needed for side batter
Offshore leads align only the hammer; a template holds the pile
Use a pile gate at the bottom of the leads

sections.title: Templates
sections.summary: Templates hold piles over water or excavations with offshore or swinging leads; top within 5 ft of cutoff or water elevation (whichever is lower), preferably at or below cutoff. Batter pile positions must allow for template elevation: a 1H:4V pile set at plan location on a template 5 ft above cutoff is 15 in. out at cutoff. Rollers preferred.
sections.body: 15.4 Templates (pp. 348 to 349). Templates hold piles in position and alignment when offshore or swinging leads are used over water or excavations (Figure 15-16). The template top should be within 5 ft of the pile cutoff elevation or the water elevation, whichever is lower, preferably at or below cutoff so final driving needs no template removal. Batter pile positions in the template depend on its elevation relative to cutoff: with the template 5 ft above cutoff and plan cutoff locations used at template level, a 1H:4V batter pile is 15 in. out of location at cutoff (Figure 15-17). Piles should pass freely without binding; templates with rollers are preferable, particularly for batter piles.
key_points: Template top within 5 ft of cutoff or water elevation (whichever is lower)
Offset batter pile positions for template elevation (1H:4V, 5 ft above cutoff: 15 in. error)
Rollers preferred so piles pass without binding

sections.title: Helmets
sections.summary: Helmets (one piece, or base helmet with insert) suit the lead, pile and hammer; they should fit loosely to avoid torsion or bending but keep alignment, about 0.1 to 0.2 in. larger than the pile; alignment is critical for precast concrete piles.
sections.body: 15.5 Helmets (pp. 349 to 351). Figure 15-18 shows helmet components and nomenclature. Configuration and size depend on lead, pile and hammer type; helmets are one piece for a specific pile or two piece (base helmet plus insert); details from manufacturers, suppliers and contractors. To avoid transmitting torsion or bending the helmet or insert should fit loosely, but not so loosely as to lose alignment: about 0.1 to 0.2 in. larger than the pile diameter; alignment is especially critical for precast concrete piles. A cracked helmet (Figure 15-19) shows striker plate, hammer cushion (two aluminum and one micarta plate) and helmet; Figure 15-20 shows one piece helmets for concrete and pipe piles; Figure 15-21 a base helmet with H-pile insert and pipe pile inserts for several diameters and walls.
key_points: One piece helmets or base helmet with insert
Helmet or insert about 0.1 to 0.2 in. larger than the pile: loose, but aligned
Hammer-pile alignment especially critical for precast concrete piles

sections.title: Hammer Cushions
sections.summary: Hammer cushions protect the hammer; durable proprietary materials (micarta, nylon, urethane, aluminum laminates) last up to 200 hours; hardwood, wood pieces, wire rope, highly elastic materials and asbestos should not be permitted (prohibited by AASHTO construction specifications); many hammers need a specific cushion thickness for timing.
sections.body: 15.6 Hammer Cushions (pp. 352 to 353). Most hammers use a hammer cushion between hammer and helmet to relieve impact shock; some need none or use a direct drive steel striker plate; ineffective cushions damage striking parts, anvil, helmet or pile. Materials are usually proprietary (micarta, nylon, urethane, other polymers) that compress and stiffen with use, eventually reducing transferred energy or increasing bending stress; they may last up to 200 hours. Old one-piece hardwood cushions about 6 in. thick, grain parallel to the pile, crush, burn and vary; hardwood, small wood pieces, wire rope or other highly elastic material should not be permitted, nor asbestos (health hazard); AASHTO LRFD Bridge Construction Specifications prohibit all of these. Man-made materials transmit energy better, keep more constant properties and last long; on smaller projects one inspection before driving may suffice, with periodic checks on larger projects; many hammers need a specific cushion thickness for proper timing. Aluminum laminates conduct heat away. Figure 15-22: Conbest and aluminum, Blue Nylon, aluminum and Micarta.
key_points: Proprietary hammer cushion materials last up to 200 hours
Do not permit hardwood, wood pieces, wire rope, highly elastic materials or asbestos
Many hammers need a specific cushion thickness for proper timing
Inspect before driving on small projects; periodically on large projects

figures.title: Typical hammer cushion materials

sections.title: Pile Cushions
sections.summary: Pile cushions protect concrete pile heads: plywood, hardwood or composites, wood at least 4 in.; replace before excessive compression or charring; after replacement ignore the first 100 blows for acceptance; wood cushions take about 1000 to 2000 blows; use a new, dry cushion for each pile.
sections.body: 15.7 Pile Cushions (pp. 353 to 354). A pile cushion between helmet and concrete pile head prevents head damage: plywood, hardwood, composites or other man-made materials; wood pile cushions at least 4 in. thick. Check periodically and replace before excessive compression or charring. After replacing a cushion during driving, do not use the blow count of the first 100 blows for acceptance, as the cushion is still absorbing energy rapidly; counts are reliable after 100 full energy blows. A wood cushion generally takes 1000 to 2000 blows in total; use a new, dry cushion for each pile, since old or water soaked cushions transfer energy poorly and deteriorate quickly (Figure 15-23: used left, new right).
key_points: Wood pile cushions at least 4 in. thick; new and dry for each pile
Ignore the first 100 blows after a cushion change for acceptance
Wood cushions generally last 1000 to 2000 blows

figures.title: Plywood pile cushions: (left) used and (right) new

sections.title: Hammers
sections.summary: Hammers are impact, vibratory or resonant; impact hammers install most foundation piles (classification Figure 15-24). Table 15-1 compares rated energy, impact velocity, blow rate, energy, power, maintenance, suitability, advantages and disadvantages for air/steam, diesel, drop, hydraulic, vibratory and resonant hammers.
sections.body: 15.8 Hammers (pp. 355 to 357). Three main types: impact, vibratory and resonant; impact hammers are the primary type, varying in power source, configuration and rated energy (classification Figure 15-24; inspection issues in Chapter 18; Rausche et al. 1986; DFI 1995). Table 15-1 (rated energy ft-kips; impact velocity ft/s; blows/min): single acting air/steam 7 to 1800; 8 to 16.5; 35 to 60, energy ram weight x stroke, versatile, simple and moderate cost, needs compressor, heavy; double acting air/steam 1 to 21; 15 to 20; 95 to 300, energy (ram weight + piston area x pressure) x stroke, more productive, some underwater; differential acting air/steam 15 to 50; 13 to 15; 98 to 300, less air than double acting; single acting (open end) diesel 9 to 1620; 10 to 16.5; 40 to 60, ram weight x stroke, stroke a function of resistance, most commonly used, variable stroke, exhaust pollution; double acting (closed end) diesel 5 to 73; 8 to 16.5; 80 to 105, (ram weight + bounce chamber pressure) x stroke, lift off in hard driving, limited availability; drop 7 to 60; 23 to 33; 4 to 8, lowest cost, not for concrete piles, very high forces and damage danger, generally obsolete; single acting hydraulic 25 to 2162; 5 to 18; 30 to 50, fully variable energy, energy readout recommended; double acting hydraulic 25 to 2581; 5 to 23; 40 to 90, underwater use, readout needed (fully enclosed); vibratory 750 to 2,400 vibrations/min, end bearing H and pipe piles in granular soils, pulling or driving, highest maintenance, not recommended for friction piles; resonant up to 10,800 vibrations/min, H and pipe piles, very low vibrations and noise, limited availability. Vibratory and resonant hammers are rated by power, not energy.
key_points: Impact hammers are the primary type for foundation piles
Table 15-1: rated energy, impact velocity and blow rate by hammer type
Single acting diesel: most commonly used; stroke varies with pile resistance
Drop hammers: very high forces, damage danger, generally obsolete
Vibratory and resonant hammers rated by power, not energy

sections.title: Hammer Energy Concepts
sections.summary: Hammer energy ratings come from dynamic formula practice: potential energy (ram weight x stroke) for gravity hammers, equivalent stroke for double acting hammers. Impact velocity Vi = sqrt(2 g h) (Eq. 15-1), kinetic energy KE = 1/2 m Vi^2 (Eq. 15-2); losses make kinetic energy less than potential, and transferred energy (ENTHRU, integral of force times velocity) is lower still.
sections.body: 15.8.1 Hammer Energy Concepts (pp. 358 to 359). Before the wave equation, criteria came from work and energy: hammer energy equated to nominal resistance times final set, leading to energy ratings and dynamic formulas, largely replaced but leaving the rating legacy. Gravity hammers (drop, single acting air/steam or hydraulic) are rated by potential energy at full stroke (ram weight w times stroke h); open end diesels are often rated by manufacturer principles, observed stroke historically ignored, now measured electronically from blow rate. Double acting hammers' downward pressure increases the equivalent stroke (that of a single acting hammer with the same impact velocity) and shortens the cycle. Ideally Vi = sqrt(2 g h) (Eq. 15-1; Vi impact velocity ft/s, g = 32.17 ft/s2, h stroke ft) and KE = (1/2) m Vi^2 (Eq. 15-2; KE ft-lbs, m ram mass). Without losses KE would equal potential energy, but friction, residual air pressure, preadmission, gas compression and pre-ignition reduce it; inspectors identify losses, contractors correct them; modern hydraulic hammers measure velocity near impact. Further losses occur in hammer cushion, helmet, pile cushion and inelastic pile head collision; energy delivered to the pile is the integral of force times velocity over time, the transferred energy or ENTHRU. Pile length, stiffness and resistance affect it; diesel stroke depends on resistance and transferred energy; double acting hammers depend on resistance through lift-off; energy transfers only while force and velocity are both positive, and with higher resistance or shorter piles rebound returns energy to the hammer, possibly before all is transferred.
key_points: Gravity hammers rated by potential energy (ram weight x stroke)
Double acting hammers rated by equivalent stroke (same impact velocity)
Losses: friction, preadmission, gas compression, pre-ignition, cushions, helmet
Transferred energy ENTHRU = integral of force x velocity over time

equations.description: Impact velocity from equivalent maximum stroke

equations.notes: pp. 358-359. With no losses kinetic energy would equal potential energy.

sections.applicability: Hammer energy rating, kinetic energy and transferred energy concepts.

sections.title: Drop Hammers
sections.summary: Drop hammers (hoist, clutch, line, weight) have variable, poorly controlled strokes, low fall efficiency and slow blow rates; the main risk is overstressing the pile, so limit the stroke. Generally limited to sheet piles; not recommended for foundation piles.
sections.body: 15.9 Drop Hammers (pp. 359 to 360). The drop hammer (Figure 15-25) is a hoisting engine with friction clutch, hoist line and drop weight; stroke is widely variable and imprecise. The clutch raises the ram, then releases it to fall as the line pays out; efficiency is low as the ram must overcome the hoist's rotational inertia, and premature or partial clutch engagement reduces it further; operating speed depends on operator skill and height of fall, generally very slow. Pile stresses rise with impact velocity, so limit the stroke to avoid damage. Inexpensive and simple but less efficient; now generally limited to sheet piles where resistance is not an issue; not recommended for foundation piles.
key_points: Variable, imprecise stroke; low fall efficiency; very slow blow rate
Main risk is overstressing the pile: limit the stroke
Not recommended for foundation piles

figures.title: Typical drop hammer

sections.title: Single Acting Air/Steam Hammers
sections.summary: Single acting air/steam hammers lift the ram by external air or steam pressure and let it fall by gravity; stroke varies with pressure, volume and pile rebound; pressure readmitted about 2 in. before impact, too early with a thin cushion (preadmission). Maximum stroke 3 to 5 ft; some have two strokes; moderate cost, simple, good for large concrete and steel piles.
sections.body: 15.10 Single Acting Air/Steam Hammers (pp. 361 to 363). Essentially drop hammers with the hoist line replaced by steam or, mostly, compressed air, using a one-cylinder engine: the ram block's ram point strikes a striker plate (Figures 15-26, 15-27(a)). Pressure on a piston raises the ram; a valve releases it and the ram coasts to maximum height, which depends on supplied pressure and volume and pile rebound, then falls by gravity less friction onto striker plate and cushion. Pressure re-enters about 2 in. before impact, depending on correct cushion thickness; too low a cushion admits it too early, reducing impact energy ('preadmission'). Force durations are as short as a drop hammer's but accelerations smaller at shorter strokes; some have two strokes selectable to limit resistance or control tension; maximum stroke generally 3 to 5 ft; rams heavier than drop hammers; moderate cost, simple operation and maintenance; suited to many piles, particularly large concrete and steel piles. Figure 15-27(b), printed here, shows the differential acting air hammer of 15.12.
key_points: Ram raised by external air/steam pressure, falls by gravity
Stroke varies with supply pressure, volume and pile rebound
Preadmission: thin cushion admits pressure too early (normally about 2 in. before impact)
Maximum stroke generally 3 to 5 ft; some hammers have two strokes

figures.title: Schematic of a single acting air/steam hammer
(a) Single acting air, and (b) differential acting air hammers

sections.applicability: Single acting air and steam hammers.

sections.title: Double Acting Air/Steam Hammers
sections.summary: Double acting air/steam hammers add upper cylinder pressure on the downstroke; pressure may need reducing in hard driving to prevent lift-off, cutting impact energy; correct cushion thickness is critical for timing. Comparable energy at up to about twice the blow rate of a single acting hammer of equal ram weight; slightly less efficient; now infrequent.
sections.body: 15.11 Double Acting Air/Steam Hammers (pp. 363 to 365). Pressure raises the ram; near the top the lower valve exhausts and the upper valve admits pressure, so gravity and upper pressure accelerate the ram down (Figure 15-28); stroke varies with pressure, volume and rebound; in hard driving pressure may need reducing to prevent lift-off (the hammer lifting off the pile), reducing impact energy; valves reverse just before impact. Correct cushion thickness is extremely important: with wrong timing the ram may run with little or no impact force. A properly operating double acting hammer delivers comparable energy per blow at up to about twice the blow rate of a single acting hammer of the same ram weight. Some are enclosed for underwater use; more dependent on air pressure, on average slightly less efficient than equivalently rated single acting hammers, cost more, need more maintenance, more air and higher pressures; use has diminished.
key_points: Upper cylinder pressure accelerates the downstroke
Reduce pressure in hard driving to prevent lift-off (reduces impact energy)
Correct cushion thickness essential for timing
Up to about twice the blow rate of a single acting hammer; slightly less efficient

figures.title: Schematic of a double acting air/steam hammer

sections.applicability: Double acting air and steam hammers.

sections.title: Differential Acting Air/Steam Hammers
sections.summary: Differential acting hammers use two pistons of different diameter with a single valve; short stroke, fast blow rate; pressure reduced in hard driving against lift-off; cushion thickness prevents preadmission; need 120 to 140 psi at the inlet, more than most compressors give (120 to 130 psi); slightly less efficient than single acting; now infrequent.
sections.body: 15.12 Differential Acting Air/Steam Hammers (pp. 366 to 367). A type of double acting hammer with short stroke and fast blow rate (Figures 15-27(b), 15-29): pressure on two different diameter pistons gives a net upward force while the upper chamber is open to atmosphere; when the valve admits pressure above, the net force turns downward, slowing the rising ram and then assisting gravity. Pressure must be reduced in hard driving to prevent lift-off, reducing impact energy; the valve reverses just before impact, so cushion thickness must prevent preadmission. Proper operation needs very high inlet pressures of 120 to 140 psi, whereas most compressors produce about 120 to 130 psi at the compressor. Efficiency is somewhat lower than the equivalent single acting hammer; the heavier ram uses less air than a double acting hammer; use has diminished.
key_points: Two different diameter pistons; short stroke, fast blow rate
Needs 120 to 140 psi at the inlet (compressors often give 120 to 130 psi)
Proper cushion thickness prevents preadmission

figures.title: Schematic of a differential acting air/steam hammer

sections.applicability: Differential acting air and steam hammers.

sections.title: Single Acting (Open End) Diesel Hammers
sections.summary: Open end diesel: ram falls, compresses air and fuel, impact and combustion drive the pile and throw the ram up; stroke depends on fuel, rings, recoil dampener, resistance and pile, so it cannot be fully controlled; pre-ignition wastes energy; may not run in easy driving. Stroke from blow rate h = 4.01 (60/bpm)^2 - 0.3 (Eq. 15-3, open end diesels only).
sections.body: 15.13 Single Acting (Open End) Diesel Hammers (pp. 368 to 370). Diesel hammers carry their own fuel (Figure 15-30): the ram is lifted on a trip block, released, and falls; fuel is injected below the air/exhaust ports, air and fuel are compressed past the ports, and on impact the fuel explodes (liquid injection, or atomized just before impact); impact and combustion drive the pile, and gas pressure and rebound throw the ram up past the ports, exhausting gases and drawing in air. Manufacturers do not agree on ratings, many using maximum stroke times ram weight; actual stroke depends on fuel charge, piston ring condition, recoil dampener thickness, driving resistance and pile length and stiffness, so it cannot be fully controlled and the maximum rated stroke may not be reached. Normally part of the energy compresses gases; when the hammer heats, fuel may ignite early ('pre-ignition'), raising pressure before impact and leaving less energy for the pile. In very easy driving the stroke may be too low to scavenge air and the hammer stops, needing repeated manual lifting. Stroke is reduced by less fuel (stepped settings, variable throttles, or a ground pump), useful for limiting stresses; stroke also rises with resistance, helping control tension in concrete piles in easy driving; it should be monitored. Stroke h (ft) = 4.01 (60/bpm)^2 - 0.3 (Eq. 15-3; bpm blows per minute), applicable only to single acting diesels. Diesels may be expensive and complex to maintain; exhaust concerns lead to kerosene, biodiesel, non-petroleum lubricants or a smokeless model, though they burn far less fuel than an air hammer's compressor; they are lighter than air hammers of similar rating (photograph in Figure 15-31(a), printed in 15.14).
key_points: Stroke depends on fuel, rings, dampener, resistance and pile: not fully controllable
Pre-ignition raises pressure before impact and reduces transferred energy
May stop running in very easy driving (insufficient scavenging)
Reduced fuel limits stresses; stroke rising with resistance helps control tension
Stroke h = 4.01 (60/bpm)^2 - 0.3 ft (Eq. 15-3), single acting diesels only

equations.description: Stroke of a single acting (open end) diesel hammer from blow rate
equations.notes: p. 370. Only for single acting diesel hammers; not correct for other hammer types.

figures.title: Schematic of a single acting diesel hammer

sections.title: Double Acting (Closed End) Diesel Hammers
sections.summary: Closed end diesel hammers compress air in a bounce chamber above the ram, shortening the stroke and raising the blow rate; fuel should be reduced so there is little or no lift-off; energy is read from peak bounce chamber pressure with the manufacturer's chart (as a function of hose length); now infrequent.
sections.body: 15.14 Double Acting (Closed End) Diesel Hammers (pp. 371 to 373). Like the open end diesel but with a closed cylinder top: the rising ram compresses air in the 'bounce chamber', shortening the stroke and raising the blow rate (Figures 15-31(b), 15-32). Ports keep atmospheric pressure until the ram top passes them; the compressed air stores energy used on the downstroke; stroke depends on fuel, pile length and stiffness, soil resistance and rings. Chamber pressure grows until the upward force balances the cylinder's weight; beyond that the hammer lifts, which causes unstable driving and damage, so fuel and combustion pressure should be reduced to give very slight or no lift-off, usually by a hand fuel pump on a hose. Energy is found from the peak bounce chamber pressure gauge and the manufacturer's chart relating the reading, as a function of hose length, to energy. Use is limited. Figure 15-31 (both diesel types) is printed in this section.
key_points: Bounce chamber shortens the stroke and raises the blow rate
Reduce fuel so there is very slight or no hammer lift-off
Energy from peak bounce chamber pressure and the manufacturer's chart (hose length)

figures.title: (a) Single acting diesel and, (b) double acting diesel hammers
Schematic of a double acting diesel hammer

sections.title: Single Acting Hydraulic Hammers
sections.summary: Single acting hydraulic hammers lift the ram hydraulically and release it to fall by gravity; stroke, blow rate and dwell time are adjustable from a pendant (very short strokes in easy driving); built-in monitors measure ram velocity before impact and should be required, with readings logged.
sections.body: 15.15 Single Acting Hydraulic Hammers (pp. 373 to 375). An external hydraulic power source lifts the ram, a modern counterpart of air/steam hammers with similar ram weights and strokes; low headroom models fit excavators, larger ones specialty rigs or leads. Actuators lift the ram and retract quickly at a set height, releasing it to fall onto striker plate and cushion; gravity alone does the work (some accumulators add a small double acting component) (Figures 15-33(a), 15-34(a)). Stroke, blow rate and dwell time are continuously varied from a pendant: very short strokes prevent pile run or limit tension in concrete piles in easy driving, higher strokes serve hard driving. Stroke can often be estimated visually, but most newer hammers have a built-in monitor of ram velocity just before impact, convertible to kinetic energy or equivalent stroke; given stroke variability it should be required and its readings recorded on the driving log. A dedicated power pack is needed; operation and maintenance can be more complex. Figures 15-33 and 15-34 also show the double acting hammer of 15.16.
key_points: Ram lifted hydraulically, falls by gravity
Stroke, blow rate and dwell time adjustable; short strokes in easy driving
Require the built-in ram velocity (energy) monitor and log its readings

figures.title: Schematic of hydraulic hammers: (a) single acting and (b) double acting
(a) Single acting hydraulic, and (b) double acting hydraulic hammers

sections.title: Double Acting Hydraulic Hammers
sections.summary: Double acting hydraulic hammers accelerate the ram down by hydraulic pressure or nitrogen, are fully enclosed (stroke not visible, so built-in monitoring is essential), can work underwater without followers, and usually give steel on steel impact without conventional cushions at high efficiency.
sections.body: 15.16 Double Acting Hydraulic Hammers (pp. 375 to 376). They cover the single acting range and can be much larger (schematic Figure 15-33(b), photograph Figure 15-34(b), both printed in 15.15). A ram on a piston rod is enclosed in the housing; oil from an external source raises the piston, then at a set height the supply valve closes and the return opens, and the ram is accelerated down by hydraulic pressure or compressed nitrogen onto the anvil and pile, steel on steel with relatively high transfer. Stroke is adjustable but not visible, so built-in monitoring is essential. Fully enclosed hammers can operate underwater, avoiding followers or extra pile length; most have no conventional hammer cushion; some drive piles horizontally.
key_points: Ram accelerated down by hydraulic pressure or compressed nitrogen
Fully enclosed: built-in monitoring essential
Can drive underwater, avoiding followers

sections.title: Vibratory Hammers
sections.summary: Vibratory hammers use counter-rotating eccentric weights: variable moment and high frequency up to 2300 to 2400 vpm (40 Hz), standard up to 1600 vpm (26 Hz), low frequency about 1200 vpm (20 Hz); lower rates affect soil and structures more (start-up and shut-down). Best in submerged granular soils; not for precast concrete; no reliable nominal resistance method.
sections.body: 15.17 Vibratory Hammers (pp. 376 to 378). Paired counter-rotating eccentric weights impose a sinusoidal axial force, horizontal components cancelling (Figures 15-35, 15-36). Types: variable moment and high frequency hammers up to 2300 to 2400 vibrations per minute (40 Hz); standard up to 1600 (26 Hz); low frequency up to about 1200 (20 Hz). Lower rates affect soil and structures more, so start-up and shut-down raise the most vibration concern; variable moment hammers reach full speed with eccentrics in neutral, avoiding critical frequencies. Clamped hydraulically to the pile head, they install or extract, usually without leads (templates for sheet pile cells); rated by energy per second and/or driving force; powered by a hydraulic pack. Common for sheet piles, also non-displacement H-piles and open end pipes; closed end pipes and displacement piles are difficult; not for precast concrete (tension and bending); most effective in granular, especially submerged, soils, possibly in silty or softer clays, less in stiff to hard clays. Wave equation programs can simulate vibratory driving and measurements have been made, but no reliable method gives nominal resistance, so confirm it by other means.
key_points: Frequencies: 40 Hz (variable moment/high frequency), 26 Hz standard, 20 Hz low frequency
Start-up and shut-down cause the most vibration concern; variable moment hammers help
Most effective in submerged granular soils; less in stiff to hard clays
Not for precast concrete piles
No reliable nominal resistance from vibratory installation: confirm by other means

figures.title: Schematic of a vibratory hammer
Vibratory hammer installing an H-pile

sections.title: Resonant Hammers
sections.summary: Resonant hammers drive a hydraulic piston at up to 180 Hz (10,800 vpm), automatically tuned to keep resonance; fast, very low vibration and reduced noise, but nominal resistance must be verified afterwards with an impact hammer.
sections.body: 15.18 Resonant Hammers (pp. 378 to 379). A hydraulic piston-cylinder with a valve rapidly switching oil to alternate sides generates a high magnitude, high frequency force oscillating at up to 180 Hz (10,800 vibrations per minute); a proprietary algorithm adjusts frequency to keep resonance (H-pile and pipe pile projects summarized by Janes 2009). Advantages: fast installation, very low ground vibration, reduced noise, standard cranes and power packs. As with vibratory piles there is no reliable resistance method, so an impact hammer and standard verification must follow installation (Figure 15-37).
key_points: Up to 180 Hz (10,800 vibrations per minute), automatically held at resonance
Fast, very low ground vibrations, reduced noise
Nominal resistance verified afterwards with an impact hammer

figures.title: Resonant hammer installing an H-pile

sections.title: Impact Hammer Size Selection
sections.summary: Select impact hammers by wave equation, not dynamic formulas; a ram weight of 1 to 2% of the required nominal (or nominal driving) resistance is a first estimate; Table 15-2 gives preliminary minimum rated energies (12,000 ft-lbs up to 180 kips to 42,000 ft-lbs at 540 to 600 kips), not for specifications.
sections.body: 15.19 Impact Hammer Size Selection (pp. 379 to 380). Too small a hammer may not reach the resistance or needs excessive blows; too large may damage the pile. Dynamic formulas should not be used to size hammers; they worsen with hammer complexity and resistance. A wave equation of the hammer-cushion-pile-soil system is recommended; a ram weight of 1 to 2% of the required nominal resistance or nominal driving resistance, whichever is greater, is often a good first estimate. Table 15-2 (nominal resistance kips: minimum manufacturer's rated energy ft-lbs): 180 and under: 12,000; 181 to 300: 21,000; 301 to 415: 28,800; 416 to 540: 37,600; 540 to 600 (as printed): 42,000; adjust for pile type, loads, lengths and soils (short piles to rock may need a smaller hammer for stresses); not for use in a specification (see Chapter 14 for developing one).
key_points: Size hammers by wave equation; dynamic formulas not recommended
First estimate: ram weight 1 to 2% of required nominal (or nominal driving) resistance
Table 15-2: preliminary minimum rated energy by nominal resistance; not for specifications

tables.title: Preliminary Hammer Energy Requirements
tables.description: Minimum manufacturer's rated energy for preliminary equipment evaluation: 180 kips and under 12,000 ft-lbs; 181 to 300 kips 21,000; 301 to 415 kips 28,800; 416 to 540 kips 37,600; 540 to 600 kips 42,000 (the print's last band starts at 540). Not for use in a specification.

sections.title: Hammer Kinetic Energy Monitoring
sections.summary: Kinetic energy readouts time the ram between proximity switches to give impact velocity and kinetic energy (and blow rate, open end diesel stroke); any hammer can be retrofitted (two 1.2 in. holes in a diesel cylinder) with a wireless E-Saximeter that also logs driving; valuable on large projects or large resistances.
sections.body: 15.20 Hammer Kinetic Energy Monitoring (pp. 380 to 383). Manufacturer devices monitor hard wired proximity switches in the hammer body; impact velocity and kinetic energy come from the ram's travel time between switches, with blow rate and, for open end diesels, stroke (IHC hydraulic panel Figure 15-38; Berminghammer diesel Figures 15-39, 15-40). Any hammer can be retrofitted: on diesels the switches sit in two 1.2 in. smooth bore holes in the cylinder wall above the combustion chamber; on air/steam or single acting hydraulic hammers they attach to the body; a transmitter sends impact velocity and kinetic energy to a wireless hand held E-Saximeter, which can also keep the driving log as the inspector keys each increment and shows open end diesel stroke (Figures 15-41, 15-42). Readouts improve quality control, especially on large projects or large resistances, and detect performance changes that may require adjusting the criterion.
key_points: Proximity switches time the ram to give impact velocity and kinetic energy
Any hammer can be retrofitted (diesel: two 1.2 in. holes above the combustion chamber)
E-Saximeter displays energy, stroke and keeps the driving log
Recommended on large projects or for large nominal resistances

sections.title: Noise Suppression Equipment
sections.summary: Impact driving noise ranges about 80 to 130 dBa; manufacturer shrouds cut about 10 dBa; combined measures (cushion material, exhaust shroud, damping compound on steel piles, impact-area shroud) gave 20 to 25 dBa; consider hammer and pile type at design in noise sensitive areas.
sections.body: 15.21 Noise Suppression Equipment (p. 384). Noise from impact driving ranges from around 80 to 130 dBa by hammer and pile type; ordinances or specifications may limit it or require shrouds. Optional devices on a few diesel and hydraulic hammers reduce noise by about 10 dBa (Figure 15-43). Combining shock absorbing cushion material, an exhaust shroud, damping compound on steel piles and a shroud around the hammer-pile impact area gave 20 to 25 dBa. Hammer and pile type also matter and should be considered in design for noise sensitive areas. (The heading prints 'SUPPRESION'.)
key_points: Impact driving noise about 80 to 130 dBa
Manufacturer noise shrouds: about 10 dBa reduction
Combined measures: 20 to 25 dBa reduction

sections.applicability: Airborne noise suppression for pile driving.

sections.title: Underwater Noise Suppression Equipment
sections.summary: Bubble curtains reduce underwater overpressures (above 4.4 psi found detrimental to fish): bubble rings around single piles, bubble walls around substructures; must fully surround the driving, with containment in currents or for batter piles; a ring cut over 22 psi to under 3 psi. A mandrel-driven air gap pile gave 21 to 23 dBa vs. 3 to 6 dBa for a bubble curtain.
sections.body: 15.22 Underwater Noise Suppression Equipment (pp. 385 to 386). Bubble curtains are sometimes required to reduce underwater sound, shock waves and overpressures affecting marine mammals and fish; overpressures over 4.4 psi have generally been found detrimental, varying with species, size and maturity. Bubble rings (around a single pile: high volume compressor, feed lines and distribution manifolds) and bubble walls (rings with a sound damping curtain, around a whole substructure). The curtain must completely surround the driving, hard with a ring in tides and currents or with batter piles, so rings are combined with containment (pile sleeve, turbidity curtain or cofferdam; Figure 15-44) or walls are used. Longmuir and Lively (2001): a ring reduced overpressures from over 22 psi to under 3 psi. A WSDOT and FHWA full scale test of a University of Washington and Marine Construction Technologies mandrel bottom-driven steel pipe pile (30 in. piles) found the mandrel-pipe air gap gave 21 to 23 dBa reduction against 3 to 6 dBa for a typical bubble curtain (the text cites Reinwall et al. 2014; the reference list prints Reinhall et al. 2014).
key_points: Underwater overpressures above 4.4 psi found detrimental to fish
Bubble rings around single piles; bubble walls around whole substructures
Curtain must completely surround the driving (containment in currents or for batter piles)
Mandrel air-gap pile: 21 to 23 dBa reduction vs. 3 to 6 dBa for a bubble curtain

figures.title: Bubble ring with containment device

sections.title: Followers
sections.summary: Followers transmit blows when the pile head is below the leads (under bridges, underwater, below grade); they cost energy and alignment (especially batter piles), so evaluate by thorough wave equation or dynamic measurements; a follower should have about the pile's stiffness per unit length; avoid them where possible (e.g., underwater hammers).
sections.body: 15.23 Followers (pp. 386 to 387). A follower is a member between hammer and pile used when the pile head is below the reach of the hammer, i.e., below the leads: under existing bridge decks, underwater or below grade (Figure 15-45(a)). Alignment, especially for batter piles, is a problem (Figure 15-45(b)); follower compression and connection losses reduce delivered energy and change the blow count for the required resistance, estimated by a thorough wave equation or field dynamic measurements. A properly designed follower has about the same stiffness per unit length as the pile it replaces; much less stiff ones should be avoided; followers need considerable maintenance and should be avoided when possible, e.g., by an underwater hammer.
key_points: Followers used when the pile head is below the leads
Energy losses and alignment problems; evaluate by wave equation or dynamic testing
Follower stiffness per unit length about equal to the pile's
Avoid followers where possible (e.g., use an underwater hammer)

figures.title: (a) Follower and (b) follower in use drving H-piles

sections.title: Jetting
sections.summary: Jetting (water or air) displaces soil, most effective in loose to medium dense granular soils; not recommended for friction piles or piles needing lateral resistance; end bearing piles must reach final resistance by driving; backfill open holes; separate pay item; now rare because of environmental restrictions unless contained.
sections.body: 15.24 Jetting (pp. 388 to 389). Water or air jets, sometimes combined, displace soil to create a pilot hole before or during placement, with pipes inside or outside the pile; most effective in loose to medium dense granular soils. Not recommended for friction piles (reduces shaft resistance) and avoided for piles providing substantial lateral resistance; end bearing piles reach final resistance by driving without jetting; backfill open holes; include a separate pay item; alternatives are predrilling and spudding. Environmental restrictions have greatly reduced jetting, rarely used without containment (dual jets on a concrete pile Figure 15-46; jet/punch Figure 15-47).
key_points: Most effective in loose to medium dense granular soils
Not recommended for friction piles or piles needing lateral resistance
Final resistance of end bearing piles obtained by driving without jetting
Rarely used now because of environmental restrictions

sections.title: Predrilling
sections.summary: Predrilling passes obstructions and embankments, limits vibration and reduces heave; hole usually 4 in. less than the diagonal of square or H-piles and 1 in. less than round pile diameter; equal to the diagonal or diameter in very hard material; up to 6 in. larger than the greatest dimension in embankments; state size and depth; separate pay item.
sections.body: 15.25 Predrilling (pp. 389 to 390). Augers or rotary drills facilitate driving or limit vibrations, pass obstructions (old timbers, boulders, riprap), penetrate embankments, and help reduce heave of closely spaced displacement piles. The hole should permit driving yet support the pile laterally, with size and depth in the contract documents: in most cases 4 in. less than the diagonal of square or steel H-piles and 1 in. less than the diameter of round piles; equal to the diagonal or diameter into or through very hard material; up to 6 in. larger than the greatest dimension in embankments. Include a separate pay item (solid flight auger Figure 15-48).
key_points: Hole 4 in. less than the diagonal (square or H-piles), 1 in. less than round pile diameter
Equal to diagonal or diameter in very hard material
Up to 6 in. larger than the greatest dimension in embankments
State hole size and depth; separate pay item

figures.title: Solid flight auger predrilling system

sections.title: Spudding
sections.summary: Spudding drives or drops a short strong member to open a hole through dense fill or debris and then removes it; a spud driven too deep may not pull out, but cuttings and groundwater stay underground (spuds in Figure 15-49, printed in 15.27).
sections.body: 15.26 Spudding (p. 390). Spudding opens a hole through dense material by driving or dropping a short, strong member and removing it, used instead of jetting or predrilling where upper soils are miscellaneous fill and debris. A spud driven too deep may not be pullable; an advantage is that cuttings and groundwater are not brought to the surface for disposal. Figure 15-49 (printed after the 15.27 heading): (a) a thick walled pipe section with a conical plate tip, (b) an H-pile section with a wedge tip and plates.
key_points: Spud driven or dropped to open a hole through fill and debris, then removed
Risk: spud driven too deep may not be pulled
No cuttings or groundwater brought to the surface

sections.title: Equipment Submittals
sections.summary: The Contractor should submit all proposed equipment and procedures and a Pile Installation Plan before driving so the Engineer can run a wave equation and set criteria; Figure 15-50 is a drive system submittal form; jetting, predrilling or spudding equipment information goes with it. Without system details wave equation accuracy drops.
sections.body: 15.27 Equipment Submittals (pp. 390 to 392). An equipment submittal of all proposed equipment and procedures should reach the Engineer before driving, with a Pile Installation Plan followed throughout, so the Engineer can evaluate equipment, run a wave equation with appropriate soil modeling and give preliminary or final criteria. Figure 15-50 is a drive system submittal form covering hammer components and accessories and pile type, section, splices and toe details; information on jetting, predrilling or spudding equipment accompanies it. The text refers to 'Section 14.2.1 and 14.2.3' for the installation plan and equipment specifications (they are printed in 14.2.2, X.02, and 14.2.4, X.04). Without specific system details the accuracy of wave equation modeling, criteria and drivability assessment is reduced (Chapter 12). The spud photographs of 15.26 (Figure 15-49) are printed in this section.
key_points: Submit all equipment, procedures and a Pile Installation Plan before driving
Figure 15-50: drive system submittal form (hammer, cushions, helmet, pile details)
Missing system details reduce wave equation accuracy
